$comment: Shared table for the HDF->SIEM exporters (hdf-to-ocsf, hdf-to-splunk, hdf-to-ecs), which emit numbers straight into NDJSON. Go (EncodeLine) and TypeScript (canonicalize + stringifyLine) both read it, so neither language can drift. 'json' is the raw JSON number text as it appears in the HDF input; 'token' is the exact token the NDJSON output must carry. Measured, not assumed: Go's encoder and JSON.stringify agree on every case below EXCEPT negative zero, including both exponent thresholds, the smallest denormal and max float. That is why negative zero is handled as a special case rather than by reformatting every number -- routing all of them through a positional formatter would BREAK the exponent rows, which currently agree.

cases.why: the defect: Go kept the sign, JSON.stringify drops it. Reachable without hand-authored input -- the shared impact rounding returns negative zero for any small negative impact in BOTH languages, so they agree on the value and parted company only at serialization. Normalized to 0 on export by decision; see $decision
positive zero is unchanged, so the normalization cannot be a blanket sign rewrite
the magnitude where both languages switch to exponent notation -- they agree, and a positional reformat would break this
the same switch on the negative side
just below the exponent threshold, where both render positionally
below the small-magnitude threshold; both use exponent, and Go trims its e-07 to e-7
at the small-magnitude boundary, where both still render positionally
smallest positive denormal -- pins that shortest-round-trip digits agree at the extreme
max finite double, the opposite extreme
an ordinary small negative -- distinguishes a real negative from negative zero
the classic binary-fraction value, pinning shortest-round-trip rather than exact expansion

floatTokenCases.why: FloatToken/floatNumber carry the same normalization in the decimal-point convention OCSF float_t needs. TypeScript already produced 0.0; Go produced -0.0 and changed
positive zero keeps the decimal point but gains no sign
a whole number must carry .0 so OCSF float_t does not see an integer-shaped token
an ordinary CVSS-shaped score already bearing a decimal point

$floatTokenComment: floatTokenCases deliberately omits exponent-range values. FloatToken (Go, strconv 'f') and floatNumber (TypeScript, String()) diverge for every value outside the positional range -- 1e21 renders 1000000000000000000000.0 in Go and 1e+21 in TypeScript -- which is a SEPARATE defect from negative zero and is not fixed here. Its only current guard is that the domain is CVSS scores in [0,10]. Do not read this table as covering it.
$decision: DECISION: negative zero is NORMALIZED to positive zero on the export path, in both languages. A sign on a zero impact carries nothing a SIEM consumer can act on and it surprises anyone diffing output, so the exporters erase it rather than propagate it. JavaScript already did this for free (JSON.stringify(-0) is '0'); Go preserved the sign, so Go is the side that changed. NOTE the deliberate asymmetry with the HASHING path: hdfutil.CanonicalJSON and canonicalJson both KEEP the sign, in both languages, because a checksum must reflect the bytes it was given. Export is a presentation boundary and hashing is an identity boundary; they are allowed to differ, and this row is the reason a future reader should not 'fix' one to match the other.
